title: M34, NGC 1039
caption: The open star cluster M34, imaged by the Burrell Schmidt telescope at Kitt Peak

recognition.text: Published in the NSF NOIRLab image archive. No published rating.

story: This approximately true-colour picture shows M34, also listed as NGC 1039, an open star cluster that lies in the direction of the constellation Perseus. Under good conditions it can be seen with the naked eye.
M34 lies some 1400 light-years away. About a hundred stars make it up, spread through a region roughly a dozen light-years across.

An open cluster is a loose group of stars that formed together from the same cloud of gas and dust. Because they share an origin, the stars have similar ages and chemical makeup, which makes such clusters useful for comparing how stars of different masses evolve. Over long stretches of time, the gravity of the rest of the Galaxy tends to pull open clusters apart, so their members gradually drift off to join the general population of stars. Compared with the dense globular clusters, open clusters are usually younger and much more loosely bound.
scale: M34 is about 1400 light-years away and some dozen light-years across, according to NOIRLab.

understand.summary: The Burrell Schmidt telescope on Kitt Peak recorded M34 in visible light through B, V and R filters, combined into an approximately true-colour picture.
understand.eye: To the naked eye M34 is a faint hazy patch; the telescope's exposures show its individual stars and their colours.

explore: The images were taken through B, V and R filters in July 1996 with Case Western Reserve University's Burrell Schmidt telescope, at its Warner and Swasey Observatory near Tucson, Arizona, on Kitt Peak, as part of the Research Experiences for Undergraduates program at Kitt Peak National Observatory. The field is 34.6 arcminutes across.
alt: A loose scattering of bright stars against a field of fainter stars.
